what_its_for: Nadolol is used to treat high blood pressure (hypertension) and to prevent chest pain (angina). It belongs to a group of medicines called beta-blockers, which work by slowing your heart rate and relaxing your blood vessels so your heart does not have to work as hard.
how_to_take: Take nadolol by mouth, with or without food. Swallow the tablet whole with a full glass of water. Try to take it at the same time every day to help you remember. Do NOT stop taking this medicine suddenly without talking to your doctor first — stopping it too quickly can cause serious heart problems.
dosing: Your doctor will decide the right dose for you. Most adults start at 40 mg once a day. Your doctor may slowly increase your dose based on how your body responds. The usual dose range is 40 mg to 320 mg once daily. Always follow your doctor's specific instructions and never change your dose on your own.
missed_dose: If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember — but only if it is still the same day. If it is almost time for your next dose, skip the missed dose and continue with your regular schedule. Never take two doses at the same time to make up for a missed one.
storage: Store nadolol at room temperature, between 68°F and 77°F (20°C and 25°C). Keep it away from heat, moisture, and direct light. Store it in a dry place, such as a dresser drawer or cabinet — NOT in the bathroom. Keep all medicines out of reach of children and pets. Do not use after the expiration date on the label.
what_to_avoid: Avoid drinking alcohol, as it can lower your blood pressure too much and cause dizziness. Do not use over-the-counter cold, flu, or allergy medicines (such as decongestants) without asking your doctor or pharmacist first, as they can raise your blood pressure or affect your heart rate. Avoid getting up too quickly from a sitting or lying position to prevent dizziness or fainting. Do not stop taking this medicine suddenly.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor right away or go to the emergency room if you experience: very slow heartbeat (fewer than 50 beats per minute), severe dizziness or fainting, sudden shortness of breath or wheezing, swelling of your hands, feet, or ankles, unusual weight gain (more than 2–3 pounds in a day or 5 pounds in a week), chest pain that gets worse, signs of low blood sugar if you have diabetes (since nadolol can hide these signs), or cold or blue fingers and toes. Also call your doctor if you feel depressed or notice any mental or mood changes.
when_it_works: For high blood pressure, nadolol begins to lower your blood pressure within a few hours of your first dose, but it may take 1 to 2 weeks of regular use before you feel the full benefit. For chest pain (angina), you should notice fewer episodes over time. Even if you feel well, keep taking this medicine — high blood pressure often has no symptoms.
special_populations: Older adults: You may be more sensitive to the effects of nadolol, especially dizziness and slow heart rate. Your doctor may start you on a lower dose. Kidney problems: Nadolol is removed from your body through your kidneys. If you have kidney disease, your doctor may need to adjust your dose or have you take it less often. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: Tell your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding. Nadolol can pass into breast milk and may affect your baby. Your doctor will help you weigh the risks and benefits. Diabetes: Nadolol can hide some symptoms of low blood sugar (like a fast heartbeat). Monitor your blood sugar closely and talk to your doctor about this. Asthma or breathing problems: Nadolol is generally NOT recommended if you have asthma or severe breathing problems, as it can make breathing worse. Tell your doctor about any lung conditions before taking this medicine.
